# Affine root-majorant contacts form a weighted singleton centroid graph

This extends the maximum-volume centroid-graph theorem to contacts of
a GLOBAL affine upper bound on intrinsic volume roots. It gives a
proved weighted face-mass guarantee. It does not assert that one such
contact set carries all the mass of a general mixed convex body.

## Theorem

Let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d and let
S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) be nonempty. Assume

    q=dim_H(S)=max_z affdim(C_z)>=1.

Let P be the finite set of nonempty integer fibers K_z=C_z. Define

    a_z=H_q(K_z), r_z=a_z^(1/q), M=sum_(z in P) a_z=H_q(S).

For lower-dimensional fibers a_z=r_z=0. The measure H_q is intrinsically
normalized; in particular it agrees with Euclidean q-volume after an
isometric identification of a q-dimensional fiber affine span.

Suppose an affine function ell:R^n->R obeys

    r_z<=ell(z) for EVERY z in P.                    (1)

Set

    E={z in P:r_z=ell(z)>0}, W_E=sum_(z in E) a_z.

If E is nonempty, there exists a single actual point y in one of its
fibers such that every CLOSED ambient halfspace H containing y has

    H_q(S intersect H)>=(gamma_q/2^n)W_E,
    gamma_q=(q/(q+1))^q.                            (2)

The normalized depth is therefore at least
(gamma_q/2^n)(W_E/M), which is at least
(gamma_d/2^n)(W_E/M). If E is empty, the displayed zero lower bound
is trivial at any point of nonempty S; no center in E is claimed.

In particular, if r_z agrees with one affine function at EVERY
positive-volume fiber, and that function majorizes the zero-volume
fibers as in (1), then W_E=M and OC follows. The volumes on E need
not be equal. A constant majorant recovers the maximum-volume theorem.

The proof uses classical Brunn--Minkowski with its positive-volume
equality case, classical Doignon, and ordinary Grunbaum. Every
additional step is proved below.

## 1. Measure and the active centroid set

Boundedness gives finite P, and each K_z is compact and convex. Its
H_q mass is positive and finite exactly when its dimension is q, and
is zero at smaller dimensions. A q-dimensional convex body contains
a q-simplex and is bounded in its affine span, proving positivity and
finiteness. Finite additivity over the disjoint lifted fibers gives
0<M<infinity. The Hausdorff dimension of the finite union is the
maximum fiber dimension, as used in the theorem.

For every z in E let g_z be the H_q centroid of K_z. It lies in K_z.
Define

    T_E={(z,g_z):z in E}, G_E=conv(T_E).             (3)

The hull G_E is compact and contained in C. Give its finite centroid
set the atomic measure

    nu=sum_(z in E) a_z delta_(z,g_z), nu(T_E)=W_E.  (4)

The unequal weights in (4) will be retained throughout the centerpoint
argument; counting measure would not give (2).

## 2. Equality for integer averages of contact fibers

Let z_1,...,z_m lie in E, let lambda_i>0 sum to one, and suppose
w=sum_i lambda_i z_i is an integer vector. Convexity of C gives

    L=sum_i lambda_i K_(z_i) subset K_w.             (5)

In particular K_w is nonempty, so w belongs to P and the GLOBAL
majorant (1) applies at w. We prove

    w in E, L=K_w,
    sum_i lambda_i g_(z_i)=g_w.                     (6)

First account for affine-span directions. Each source K_(z_i) has
dimension q because r_(z_i)>0. Its direction space is
V_i=lin(K_(z_i)-K_(z_i)). The affine direction of L is
V_1+...+V_m: fixing the other summands shows inclusion of each V_i,
and the reverse inclusion is immediate. Since L lies in the integer
fiber K_w, whose dimension is at most q, their sum has dimension at
most q. Each V_i already has dimension q, so all these direction
spaces coincide with one q-dimensional space V. K_w also has that
dimension and direction. This rules out mixing transverse intrinsic
fibers without tracking the resulting dimension.

Translate the source bodies into V and identify V isometrically with
R^q. These translations and this identification preserve every H_q
volume; no integer-coordinate transformation is made. Brunn--Minkowski,
the affine contact identities, and (1) now give the complete chain

    r_w >= H_q(L)^(1/q)
        >= sum_i lambda_i r_(z_i)
         = sum_i lambda_i ell(z_i)
         = ell(w)
        >= r_w.                                    (7)

Every term is equal and positive. Thus w belongs to E. The positivity
also shows why a zero value of ell elsewhere cannot create a missing
case: ell(w) is a convex average of strictly positive contact values.

Equality of the positive q-volumes in (5) implies L=K_w. For a direct
justification, a point of K_w outside the compact convex L can be
strictly separated from L. A sufficiently small convex mixture of
that point with an interior ball of K_w gives a positive-radius ball
in K_w outside L. Hence a proper inclusion would strictly increase
q-volume, contradicting (7).

Equality in positive-volume Brunn--Minkowski implies the source bodies
are positively homothetic after translation into V. The many-summand
assertion follows by induction: group one body against the normalized
average of the others. The two inequalities making up the total
Brunn--Minkowski bound must both be equalities, forcing equality for
the grouped average and positive homothety in the outer two-body
step. For q=1 the same conclusion holds directly for intervals.

Consequently, in the original R^d coordinates, write

    K_(z_i)=rho_i B+t_i, rho_i>0

for one convex body B in a q-dimensional affine space. Convexity gives

    L=(sum_i lambda_i rho_i)B+sum_i lambda_i t_i.

Centroids commute with translation and positive homothety, so its
centroid is exactly sum_i lambda_i g_(z_i). Since L=K_w, (6) follows.
No general Minkowski additivity of centroids has been assumed.

## 3. Singleton integer sections and relative Helly

Every point of G_E is a finite convex combination of its listed
centroids. If its base w is integer, delete zero weights and apply
(6). The point is then exactly (w,g_w), with w in E. Conversely every
listed centroid belongs to G_E. Therefore

    G_E intersect (Z^n x R^d)=T_E,                 (8)

and all its nonempty integer sections are singletons. Also
conv(E) intersect Z^n=E. Empty original fibers cannot be introduced
because (5) makes any such integer average nonempty, while zero-volume
original fibers cannot occur because (7) makes it positive.

For completeness this singleton property gives a Helly number at
most h=2^n for the finite set T_E. Given finitely many closed convex
ambient sets A_i, let Q_i be the base projection of G_E intersect A_i.
They are compact convex sets, possibly empty. A common integer point
of the Q_i gives the SAME point in all G_E intersect A_i, by (8).
Thus an empty intersection of the A_i with T_E is equivalent to an
empty integer intersection of the Q_i. Doignon supplies at most 2^n
such Q_i, and the corresponding A_i already miss T_E. When n=0,
T_E has one point and the assertion holds directly with h=1.

## 4. Weighted centerpoint with closed boundary mass

Consider every closed ambient halfspace A satisfying

    nu(A)>(1-1/h)W_E.

Any at most h of these sets have a common point of T_E: the union
of their omitted atomic masses has total strictly less than W_E.
Section 3 gives the finite intersection property for the entire
family. Since T_E is finite, their full intersection contains some
y in T_E; otherwise one could select one excluding set per point
and obtain a finite empty intersection.

For every closed halfspace H containing y, it follows that

    nu(H)>=W_E/h.                                   (9)

Indeed, if nu(H)<W_E/h, its open complement contains more than
(1-1/h)W_E of the finite atomic mass. Move its boundary slightly into
that open complement to produce a CLOSED parallel halfspace containing
all those finitely many points and disjoint from H. It belongs to the
preceding family but omits y, a contradiction. Thus atoms on cap
boundaries have been handled explicitly, not discarded.

## 5. Actual fiber volume in every ambient cap

The selected y is (w,g_w) for w in E, so y belongs to the original
mixed set S. Fix any closed ambient halfspace H containing y. For
each (z,g_z) in T_E intersect H, restrict the cap to aff(K_z).
If its normal is nonzero on the q-dimensional direction space,
ordinary Grunbaum gives

    H_q(K_z intersect H_z)>=gamma_q a_z.

If the restriction is constant, centroid containment implies the
whole fiber is contained, with mass a_z. This includes caps whose
boundary contains the entire intrinsic fiber. Thus all continuous,
vertical and oblique ambient orientations obey the same lower bound.

Summing over the centroid points retained by H, and keeping all other
original contributions nonnegative, proves

    H_q(S intersect H)>=gamma_q nu(H)
                         >=(gamma_q/2^n)W_E.

This is (2). Since q<=d and gamma_q>=gamma_d, it implies the stated
version with gamma_d as well.

## 6. Why an arbitrary affine agreement set is insufficient

The global majorant condition is substantive. For example, take the
rational body in `candidate a1e40e6e6a2316e4`:
over the corners of [0,2]^2, place unit intervals centered at +1,-1,-1,+1,
and take their lifted convex hull. Its eight boundary integer fibers
have length one, but its central fiber has length three. For q=1,
the affine function ell=1 agrees with r_z at all eight boundary
indices but FAILS to majorize the central root r_(1,1)=3.

The convex hull of those boundary centroids has at its central
integer section the two diagonal averages +1 and -1. It is not a
singleton graph. This pinpoints the failed inequality in (7) when
an arbitrary affine agreement set is substituted for a global upper
contact set.

For q=0 the root r_z=a_z^(1/q) is undefined, so this theorem makes no
claim using that notation. The separate counting/singleton theorem
already handles q=0 and d=0. For n=0 the present theorem reduces to
ordinary Grunbaum on the single positive fiber. For 0<q<d all affine
direction changes and zero-mass fibers were addressed above.

The theorem does not partition all mass into compatible contact faces,
choose one center valid across different faces, or assert that an
affine majorant exists whose contact set has W_E=M for a general
body. The factor W_E/M is retained unless that last property is
actually part of the given geometry.
